newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cocoa prices boosted by El Nino factor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cocoa prices boosted by El Nino factor.

text.p: World prices for cocoa beans soared on Thursday as speculators focused on the potential impact of a developing "El Nino" weather pattern in the southern Pacific Ocean.
In an "El Nino" year, which does not occur very frequently, warming ocean temperatures off the western coast of South America can affect weather patterns worldwide for upto 18 months.
Cocoa traders were concerned that their fragile crop, grown in volume in only a few tropical countries, could be particularly vulnerable, mainly to drought.
Larry Acker, analyst at 3F Forecasts in Polo, Illinois, in a May newsletter said he expected, as a result of El Nino, unstable and dry weather in West Africa in coming months.
In London, September cocoa futures rose 62 stg a tonne at one stage in very heavy turnover to reach a contract high of 1,107 stg a tonne, before gains were trimmed slightly by profittaking.
"Concerns about this season and next seasons crop underly the move....," said Refco New York analyst Jim Steel.
The coffee market managed to stage a rally after recent sharp losses and London's robusta July futures gained $55 by the close to $1,760 a tonne.
"We've seen a bit of buying from the trade attracted by the lower levels, but I don't think we are looking at El Nino. We are more concerned with Brazilian weather now,' a trader said.
He was refering to the annual threat of frost to the coffee crop in world number one producer, Brazil.
In industrial metals copper jumped sharply in morning trade to a fresh one year high but could not sustain the levels later in the day.

Copper soared $50 a tonne to stand above $2,600 but the buying appeared to consist of a sizeable amount of shortcovering and short term speculative interest, and when this was completed the price fell back.
Shipping problems at a big mine in Paua New Guinea had the potential to cause some supply disruptions in the current tight copper market, but so far there was no direct impact, traders said.
In Chicago, wheat futures dropped in morning trade as the U.S. Department of Agriculture put U.S. winter wheat production above most analysts expectations.
July dropped six cents a bushel to $3.58.
